opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a useful comparison, though you have to be careful about what you're measuring. The human genome is about three billion base pairs, which works out to something like 750 megabytes of raw information. Most of that isn't doing much, though. The part that seems to be under strong selection, the part that's actually functional, is a lot smaller, maybe tens of megabytes. And the part that specifies how the brain gets wired up and how it learns is some fraction of that.

So if you ask how complex the brain's "learning algorithm" is, the genome gives you an upper bound. It's on the order of megabytes. That's comparable to, or maybe a bit bigger than, the codebase for a modern ML system, if you count the architecture, the optimizer, the training setup, all the little tricks. It's not wildly different in scale. That's one of the reasons I don't find it implausible that humans could write down something roughly as good as what evolution found. We aren't trying to reverse-engineer a hundred trillion synapses. We're trying to find a relatively compact procedure that, given lots of experience, produces something smart.

The caveat is that bits in the genome aren't the same as bits in our code. Evolution had an enormous amount of search behind those megabytes, and the genome sits on top of a huge amount of "free" structure from chemistry and development. A short instruction in DNA can unfold into something very elaborate because the physics does a lot of the work. So the description length can understate how hard the thing was to find. Evolution also wasn't optimizing for anything like compactness or legibility, so some of what's encoded is probably very specific priors, innate drives, reflexes, sensory processing, rather than a clean general learning rule.

My overall view is that the genome comparison is mildly reassuring for the view that general intelligence doesn't require some vast, irreducible amount of hand-designed complexity. Most of the complexity in a mature brain comes from learning, from the data. That fits with what we've seen in ML, where relatively simple algorithms plus scale and data take you surprisingly far. Where I'd stay uncertain is how much of the genome's contribution is clever inductive bias we haven't discovered yet, versus stuff we can make up for with more compute and more data. Empirically it's looked more like the second, but I wouldn't claim to be confident about that.

r001.rationale: The response says the genome’s relevant information is on the order of megabytes and is comparable to, or perhaps a bit larger than, a modern ML system’s codebase. It does not say the genome contains far more information than a training algorithm’s specification.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that the genome is just not that big. It's on the order of a few gigabytes, and the vast majority of that is not doing anything that looks like specifying an algorithm for learning. Most of it is about building a body, running metabolism, immune systems, that kind of thing. The part that's actually specifying how the brain gets wired up and how it learns is some much smaller fraction, and even that is operating at a very indirect level — it's specifying developmental programs that then unfold, rather than writing down weights or anything like that.

So when people say the human brain is this incredibly complex object that we're nowhere near replicating, I think there's an ambiguity. The trained brain, the adult human, is extremely complex — there's a huge amount of information in there. But almost all of that came from learning during a lifetime, from interacting with the world. The information that evolution actually put in, the prior, the learning algorithm, the architecture, is bounded by what fits in the genome, and realistically it's a lot less than that.

And if you compare that to the machine-learning algorithms we design, the code for a modern learning system is also quite small. The algorithmic content of something like a transformer plus its training setup — you could write it down in a modest number of pages. Most of the complexity is in the trained artifact, which again is the same situation as with the brain. So I actually think the two are more comparable than people tend to assume. Evolution had a lot of compute to search over that small space of algorithms, and it was searching with a pretty weak optimizer over a very long time. Humans are searching with a much stronger optimizer — we can reason about what we're doing — but over a much shorter time.

The thing I'd take from that is that I don't think there's some vast reservoir of algorithmic insight hidden in the genome that we'd need to recover before we could build systems that learn as well as humans. It seems more likely that the gap, to the extent there is one, is a modest number of ideas plus a lot of compute and data. That's part of why I've tended to think timelines aren't necessarily as long as the "the brain is unfathomably complex" intuition would suggest. Although I'd also say I hold that with a fair amount of uncertainty — it's possible that the small amount of information in the genome is doing something quite clever that's hard to find by the kind of search we're doing.

r001.rationale: The response describes the genome as a few gigabytes and the learning system’s algorithm as a modest number of pages, but calls them more comparable than people assume. It does not clearly state that the genome contains far more encoded information than the algorithm specification.

astra-6.text:
I think the genome is some evidence that the algorithms involved in intelligence aren’t extraordinarily complicated. You have this relatively small amount of information that specifies how to build a human, including the learning process that eventually produces a human mind. And only some of that information is devoted to the brain.

But you have to be careful about what you’re comparing. The genome doesn’t encode all the things a person knows. It encodes a process that learns from a huge amount of experience. So comparing the size of the genome to the number of parameters in a neural network is a little misleading. The closer comparison is to the code for the learning algorithm, together with the architecture and whatever other machinery gets learning off the ground.

And there’s still a pretty big range between ‘a few simple ideas’ and ‘a large collection of carefully engineered mechanisms.’ The genome is small enough to make me think we can eventually reproduce the relevant functionality, but large enough that it doesn’t establish that there’s just one trick we’re missing.

The other complication is that evolution was optimizing under very different constraints. It had to produce something that develops reliably, runs on very little power, and keeps an organism alive while it learns. We don’t necessarily have to reproduce all of that complexity to get a system that can do the cognitive tasks we care about.

r001.rationale: The response says the genome contains a relatively small amount of information and compares it with learning-algorithm code, but it does not state that the genome encodes far more information than a human-designed training algorithm.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the striking thing is how little information is in the genome compared to how much ends up in a human brain. You have roughly a billion bytes in the genome, and only some fraction of that is specifying how the brain develops. So it can’t be specifying everything you know or every connection in your brain. It has to be specifying some process that learns those things.

That makes me sympathetic to the idea that the algorithms involved could be relatively simple. But there’s a big gap between “simple compared to a trained human brain” and “simple compared to the learning algorithms we write down.” You could fit an enormous amount of machinery into even a small fraction of the genome—much more than the core of a typical machine-learning algorithm.

And evolution has had an opportunity to build in all kinds of useful structure: what you pay attention to, what you’re motivated to learn, how different parts of your brain interact. We shouldn’t assume that all of that reduces to one very elegant learning rule. At the same time, the size of the genome doesn’t establish that you need all that machinery to get intelligence. It’s one particular solution that evolution found, under a lot of constraints that are different from ours.

r001.rationale: The response says that even a small fraction of the genome could encode much more machinery than the core of a typical machine-learning algorithm, and contrasts this with algorithms humans write down.
